examples: Every time I see my nephew, he's grown taller.

Every time there's a bargain sale, I end up buying things I don't even need.

fields.explain:
Used to emphasize the "each time" nature of A; B repeats correspondingly and is usually a natural consequence.
Objective, neutral nuance; suitable in both spoken and written language.
Can express emotions or memories that come back each time A happens (見るたびに、思い出す...).
Not used with long-lasting states like いつも～だ (because たびに emphasizes "each time", not "all the time").

• Meaning: "Every time… , …"; emphasizes repetition for each occurrence of A, which brings about B.
• Features:

B happens repeatedly, corresponding to each occurrence of A (regular per occurrence, not necessarily at regular time intervals).
Usually used for events that can be counted in "times"; not used for continuous, long-lasting states.
B can be an emotion that arises spontaneously when A happens: ～を見るたびに、～を思い出す。

• Usually used for events that can be counted in "times"; not used for continuous, long-lasting states.
• B can be an emotion that arises spontaneously when A happens: ～を見るたびに、～を思い出す。
• Restrictions:

Not used when A is something almost constant / without "each time" boundaries.

• Not used when A is something almost constant / without "each time" boundaries.

fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～とき／～たら.
→ ～たびに means "every time… , …", with regular repetition.
2) The second clause is usually a repeated reaction/result.
→ Usually not used to describe a single occurrence.
3) Avoid using it for something that happened only once.
→ If it only means "after…" (time sequence), use a different pattern.
meaning_vi: 「～のとき、毎回同じように…する。」 毎回同じだということを特に言いたいときに使う。日常の当然のことには使わない。～・ …には状態を表す文は来ない。
When ~, … happens the same way as every time.
This structure is used when you especially want to express that it is the same every time.
This structure is not used for things that are obvious in everyday life.
~ and … do not take sentences expressing states.
examples: 1. この地方は台風が来るたびに大水の害が起こる。
In this region, every time a typhoon comes, there is flood damage.
2. 母は私が電話をかけるたびに、ちゃんとご飯を食べているかと聞く。
Every time I call my mother, she asks whether I'm eating properly.
3. このチームは試合のたびに強くなっていく。
This team gets stronger with every match.
examples: 1. ①　コンビニへ行くたびに
Every time I go to the convenience store...
2. ②　コンビニへ行くたびに、つい買いすぎてしまう。
Every time I go to the convenience store, I end up buying too much.
3. ③　最近、試合のたびにけがをしているので、気をつけよう。
Lately I've been getting injured every time I play a match, so I should be careful. meaning_vi: Every time, each time ⏐ explain: Used when talking about something that usually happens each time a particular situation occurs ⏐ examples: 1. 買い物のたびに、袋をたくさんもらう。
Every time I go shopping, I get lots of bags
2. この曲を聞くたびに、ふるさとを思い出す。
Every time I hear this song, I remember my hometown
mistakes: Incorrect use with an adjective: × 高いたびに → correct: 値段が高くなるたびに… (turned into a verb)
Confusion with ～ごとに: if it is not a regular unit (every three hours), prefer ～たびに.
Use for a constant state: × 彼はいつも忙しいたびに → いつも expresses a habit and does not combine with たびに.
B happens only once: × 日本に行くたびに、初めて富士山を見た → logical contradiction.

fields.explain: ◎ Means "enough to do something". This is an expression of degree that follows nouns referring to strength, money, time, courage, determination, etc.

examples: A dusty room / muddy shoes
My math test answers were full of mistakes.
My grandfather, who worked hard all his life, has stiff, wrinkled hands.
The path to the summit is covered in pebbles.
My father's room is so full of books that there's nowhere to step.
My shoes are covered in mud.
fields.explain:
Usually used with nouns that carry a sense of "dirt/errors/problems": 泥、ほこり、シミ、血、ミス、誤字、矛盾、偏見.
Hard to use with a positive meaning: ×賞賛だらけ → sounds odd; ばかり/いっぱい are more suitable.
The form "NだらけのN" is very common in everyday spoken and written language.
Emphasizes a feeling of discomfort, irritation, or disappointment.

• Expresses a state of being "full of, covered in, all over with" something undesirable: dirt, errors, scratches, etc.
• Strong negative nuance: the speaker evaluates it unfavorably (dirty, bad, full of problems).
• Different from "いっぱい/たくさん": emphasizes "everywhere" and "deserving criticism".
• Used for both physical things (泥、血、ほこり) and abstract things (ミス、文法の誤り、矛盾).
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused: ～だらけ and ～まみれ.
→ ～だらけ: "full of / all", usually with a negative meaning; often used for mistakes, flaws, bad things.
2) Not used for good or neutral results.
→ For "full of people, full of flowers…", a different pattern is usually used depending on the context.
3) Often used with nouns meaning "errors, trouble".
→ For example: 間違いだらけ, ごみだらけ… meaning_vi: Full of, all ～ ⏐ explain: Talks about dirty or unpleasant things that are all over or stuck all over a surface. Or describes something full of bad or unfortunate things. ⏐ examples: 1. この手紙の日本語は間違いだらけだ。
The Japanese in this letter is full of mistakes.
2. ちゃんとたたんでおかなかったから、服がしわだらけになってしまった。
I didn't fold my clothes properly, so they ended up all wrinkled.
mistakes: Attaching to verbs/adjectives: × 疲れるだらけ → correct: 疲れだらけの顔 (nominalization).
Use with a positive meaning: × 褒め言葉だらけ → sounds jarring; use 褒め言葉が多い/いっぱい.
Confusion with まみれ: 泥だらけ/泥まみれ are both fine; but ミスまみれ is unnatural, it must be ミスだらけ.
The JLPT often tests the "obligatory negative" nuance of だらけ compared with いっぱい/ばかり.

rows: Something stuck on a surface (blood, oil); rarely abstract
Spoken/written; used for a uniform theme, not necessarily negative

fields.meaning:
Confirming information
Recalling the past | A spoken-language grammar pattern for asking to confirm information you have forgotten.
examples: "The report is due next Monday, right?"
"What time does the exam start again?"
"Huh? Did I say something like that?"
"Yamada's house is near the station, isn't it?"
"Isn't Kim good at math?"
When I was a child, I used to play in this park a lot.
fields.explain:
Used to ask again in order to confirm information you already know or have heard.
Used to recall something that happened in the past.
fields.notes:
1) The two uses of ～っけ are easily confused.
→ One is asking again to confirm; the other is recalling something to yourself (reminiscing).
2) Used only in spoken language.
→ Common in conversation; not used in formal written language.
3) Usually used with the past form or with content already known.
→ Used when the speaker "knew it but has forgotten / isn't sure".
meaning_vi: …right?, confirming again
explain: Used when the speaker is unsure / vaguely remembers and wants confirmation.
Often used with questions containing question words: 何、どこ、いつ、誰＋～だっけ？
Can be used as a monologue: 電気消したっけ？ (Did I turn off the light?)
examples: 1. 明日の集合時間、何時だっけ？
What time are we meeting tomorrow again?
2. あの店、定休日は火曜だったっけ？
That shop is closed on Tuesdays, isn't it?
3. 彼、結婚してたっけ？
Is he married?
4. この漢字、どう書くんだっけ？
How do you write this kanji again?
5. 出発は９時でしたっけ？
We're leaving at 9, right?
6. ここ、前に来たっけ？それとも初めてだっけ？
Have I been here before? Or is this my first time? explain: Used to confirm a matter, thing, or feature once again
Usually used in everyday, casual spoken language ⏐ examples: 1. 国へ帰るのは、来週だ（った）っけ？
You're going back to your country next week, right?
2. 明日のパーテイーのこと、話し（まし）たっけ？
Did I tell you about tomorrow's party?
mistakes: Use in formal language/exams: × 何時でしょうかっけ → incorrect; choose でしょうか or でしたっけ depending on the context.
Wrong tense combination: × 高いだったっけ → with Aい use 高かったっけ／高いっけ.
Confusing the purpose: ～っけ is "recalling", not a neutral information question.
JLPT listening can trick you with ですか vs でしたっけ; pay attention to the nuance of recalling.

examples: It's been raining nonstop all week, so the laundry won't dry.
The Shinkansen was crowded, so I had to stand the whole three hours to Osaka.
She leaves the water running the whole time she's brushing her teeth. That's a waste of resources.
Orders for the new product are pouring in. The phone has been ringing nonstop since this morning.
Left as it is after doing it, without cleaning up afterward
The door is left open / has been left open / a window left open
fields.explain:
Often used with verbs that create a state, such as "open/close/put/turn on/turn off/take out/put in": 開ける／閉める／出す／つける／消す／置く／履く など.
A tone of criticism/reminder: ～っぱなしだ/～っぱなしにする carries a negative meaning.
Used for prolonged postures: 立ちっぱなし／座りっぱなし／歩きっぱなし → implies tiredness/discomfort.
Everyday spoken language, not very formal; neutral in written language when describing a situation.

• Meaning 1: Leaving (neglecting) the state after doing V as it is, without dealing with it further. Nuance: carelessness, annoyance, being criticized.

Analysis: emphasizes the resultant state after action V and its unexpectedly long duration.
• Meaning 2: Keep doing V / doing V continuously (for a long time). Nuance: hardship, discomfort, not changing posture/state.
• Grammar: The whole phrase functions as a noun; it can combine with にする／にしておく to emphasize the intention of "just leaving it as is".
• Restrictions: Not used for desirable, positive states (unless there is a clear intention and no criticism).
fields.notes:
• Phonetically, the geminate "っ" emphasizes a feeling of "left there / left hanging".
• Often appears in instructions/signs: 水を出しっぱなしにしないでください。
• Usually written in hiragana; the kanji form ～放し is rare and tends to look stiff/hard to read.
• Can be combined as っぱなしにしておく to emphasize "deliberately leaving it as is".
mistakes: Incorrect combination directly with a noun: ×雨っぱなし → it would have to be 雨を降らせっぱなし（unnatural）. Use the correct base verb.
Confusion with ～まま: 開けっぱなし（implies carelessness） ≠ 開けたまま（neutral, descriptive).
Forced use for a positive meaning: ×音楽を流しっぱなしで集中できた → っぱなし usually does not go with a positive result.
Choice of verb: Punctual verbs are hard to use with っぱなし if they do not produce a lasting state.

fields.meaning: While (you're at it), on the occasion of
examples: While I was out shopping, I stopped by the dry cleaner's and picked up my finished laundry.
While I was downtown on an errand, I took a look around an art museum.
(To someone making copies) "Excuse me, could you do this one too while you're at it?"
"I'll go to the department store for you today." "Are you sure?" "It's fine, I'm going that way anyway."
While you're going to the post office, could you buy some postcards for me?
While I was returning books to the library, I checked out the new arrivals.
fields.explain:
Nuance of "taking the chance / while at it", reducing the sense of making a separate effort for B.
Suitable in both spoken and written language; politeness is not affected.
Often used in gentle requests: ～ついでに、～てくれる？／～ていただけますか。

• Meaning: "While (doing) A, also do B"; B is an additional action done by taking advantage of the opportunity.
• Features:

A is the main purpose; B takes advantage of the opportunity of A (usually by the same person).
Close in time: while going to/arriving at/doing A, or just before/after A.

• A is the main purpose; B takes advantage of the opportunity of A (usually by the same person).
• Close in time: while going to/arriving at/doing A, or just before/after A.
• Restrictions: Not used when B is the main thing and A is just an excuse. Not used when the two subjects are different (unless the context allows it).
fields.notes:
• V辞書形＋ついでに emphasizes "before doing A, also…"; Vた形＋ついでに emphasizes "having done A, also…".
• When making a request, add ついでで悪いけど… to be more polite: "Sorry to ask while you're at it, but…".
• For trips: ～に行くついでに often goes with a destination/route.
meaning_vi: 「～するとき、その期間を利用して…もする。」二つの別々のことを同時にやってしまうと言いたいときに使う。～が本来の行為、…はそれに加えてする、目的のある意志的行為。
When doing ~, take advantage of that opportunity to also do ….
Used when you want to say you get two separate things done at the same time.
~ is the original action; … is an additional action, a volitional action with a purpose.
examples: 1. 散歩のついでにこのはがきをポストに出してきて。
While you're out for a walk, could you drop this postcard in the mailbox?
2. 玄関の掃除をするついでに靴の整理をしよう。
While cleaning the entrance, let's tidy up the shoes too.
3. インターネットで本を注文したついでに新しく出たDVDも調べた。
While ordering a book online, I also looked up newly released DVDs.
mistakes: Reversing main and secondary: × 買い物のついでに旅行に行く → a trip cannot be something done "while you're at" shopping.
Different subjects cause ambiguity: × 私が行くついでに、彼が荷物を受け取る → the agent should be the same.
Confusion with ながら: ～ついでに does not express simultaneity, but taking advantage of an opportunity.
JLPT: a trap choosing among ところで/ながら/ついでに; tests understanding of the relation A (main) – B (secondary).

rows: While doing A, also do B
B is secondary, done while at it

examples: I'm preparing my presentation while checking the materials.
Although I felt anxious about the future, I started a new challenge.
Despite knowing the risks, I accepted the plan.
I noted down the key points while listening to him.
Reflecting on the past while moving forward.
Despite worrying about her health, she competed in the tournament.
fields.explain:
Formal style, used in reports, essays, and the news.
With the concessive meaning, often used in set phrases: 知りつつ、分かりつつ、危険と知りつつ、心配しつつ.
Not followed directly by a command/volition after つつ; if you need to give instructions, use ～ながら or a separate sentence.
The two parallel actions may not be completely simultaneous but take place in the same period.

• Simultaneity: performing two actions in parallel, consciously. Formal, crisp nuance.
• Concession: "although knowing/aware that ..., ...". Often used with verbs of perception: 知る、思う、感じる、悩む.
• Same subject for both clauses. Unlike ～ながら, つつ is rarely used in everyday conversation.
• Not used for momentary, sudden actions; suitable for prolonged, purposeful processes.
fields.notes:
• The form "Vます＋つつも" is the classic formula for a contrast between awareness and action.
• Often seen in company documents: 検討しつつ、改善を進める／注意しつつ運用する.
• If the two actions have different agents, switch to ～ながら or a separate clause with its own subject.
mistakes: Using different subjects: × 彼は話しつつ、私はメモした → Use ながら or two independent sentences.
Using with punctual actions: × 立ち上がりつつ飛び出した → unnatural.
Adding a command right after つつ: × 注意しつつ来なさい → wrong nuance.
Confusion with つつある: つつ＝simultaneity/concession; つつある＝progression.

rows: Written language, same subject, no commands
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
Different meaning: a developing change, not "doing while doing"
Written language; does not require the same subject

fields.meaning: In other words, in short, that is
examples: He is my father's younger brother; in other words, my uncle.
This store only accepts cash. In other words, cards aren't accepted.
It means a three-tenths discount, that is, 30% off.
So in short, this failure was caused by a lack of preparation.
He said he wasn't coming. That means we'll be going by ourselves.
fields.explain:
Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence or mid-sentence, with a comma before/after to separate ideas.
Used in both speech and writing. In formal language, "すなわち/要するに" can replace it depending on the context.
When stating a strong conclusion: つまり～ということだ／わけだ to make the reasoning clear.
Do not say "つまりに/つまりな" (it is not a particle but an adverb/discourse marker).

• Rephrasing/explaining: Used to switch from way of saying A to an easier-to-understand way of saying B.
• Summary/conclusion: Wraps up after presenting reasons and facts.
• Definition/equivalence: "A, that is, B".
• Discourse nuance: Introduces the speaker's conclusion; sounds logical and coherent.
fields.notes:
• The spelling "詰まり" (noun: blockage) differs from "つまり" (adverb: in short). In conversation, both are pronounced the same and are distinguished by context/kanji.
• When linking explanations smoothly: A。つまり、B。You can also write A、つまり、B for a lighter break.
• Adding "ということだ/わけだ/ってことだ" gives a sense of affirming the inferred conclusion. explain: Used to restate a thing or matter with an equivalent, different way of saying or naming it ⏐ examples: 1. 父の兄、つまり私の伯父は、医者をしている。
My father's older brother, that is, my uncle, is a doctor
2. 田中さんは、携帯もパソコンも持っていない。つまり、メールで連絡はできないのだ。
Tanaka has neither a cell phone nor a computer. In other words, you can't contact him by email
mistakes: Confusion with "結局": "結局" is the outcome after a process; "つまり" is rephrasing/equating ideas.
Omitting the preceding clause before "つまり": you need content A to rephrase as B.
Using "つまりに": grammatically incorrect (it does not take a particle).
Overuse in formal written language: consider "すなわち/要するに" depending on the nuance.

rows: Strong generalization; slightly more formal in writing/speech

Outcome after a course of events; not "in other words"
